title: Inline completions
description: Inline completions (ghost text) predict the next code as you type: the model sees the prefix (and retrieved context), proposes a completion, and you accept with Tab. The serving constraints are brutal — <100ms to first token — so models are small, distilled, and cached aggressively. Acceptance rate is the metric; everything optimizes for it.
mechanism: Prefix + context -> small code model -> ranked completions -> ghost text render. Debounce; cancel on type; cache by prefix. <100ms budget.
algo: O(1) per keystroke (debounced); small models, big caches.

title: Ghost text UX
description: Ghost text UX is the difference between helpful and annoying: the completion renders dimmed/inline (not a popup), accepts partially (word by word), and never fights the user (typing dismisses cleanly). The rules: show only high-confidence completions, never more than ~a screen, and make dismissal free. A bad ghost text is worse than none — it trains users to ignore the feature.
mechanism: Inline dimmed render; Tab = accept (full or word); typing = dismiss; confidence threshold for showing. Never modal, never stealing focus.
demo:
print('GHOST TEXT RULES')
print('render: inline + dimmed (not a popup; never steals focus)')
print('accept: Tab (full) / ctrl+right (word-by-word)')
print('dismiss: keep typing (free); Esc (explicit)')
print('show only if confidence > threshold (a bad ghost trains ignore)')
print('length: ~a screen max; multi-line only when very confident')
print('annoying ghost text is worse than none')

title: Chat sidebars
description: Chat sidebars put conversational AI beside the work: ask about the code, get explanations, request edits applied to the editor. The sidebar shares context with the editor (open files, selection) — that shared context is what makes it useful rather than a generic chatbot. Edits apply as diffs the user reviews, never silent rewrites.
mechanism: Sidebar UI + editor context providers -> model -> responses with code blocks; 'apply' creates editor diffs. Conversation scoped to the workspace.
algo: O(context) prompt build; edits as diffs.
demo:
# sidebar shares editor context: selection + open file frame the question
context = {'file': 'main.py', 'selection': 'def fib(n): ...', 'lang': 'python'}

def ask(question):
    prompt = '[%s:%s] selection: %s\nQ: %s' % (
        context['file'], context['lang'], context['selection'], question)
    return 'answer grounded in: %s...' % prompt[:60]

print(ask('why is this slow?'))
print('shared context (not a generic chatbot); edits apply as REVIEWABLE diffs')

title: Context providers
description: Context providers feed the model what it needs: the current file, related files (imports, tests), docs, terminal output, selected code. The provider ranks by relevance and fits the budget (tokens). Good providers are why the AI seems smart — the model is only as good as its context. Providers are also the privacy boundary: each declares what it shares.
mechanism: Providers: {name, priority, get_context()} -> ranked, budgeted assembly. @-mentions for explicit inclusion. Each provider declares its data source (privacy).
demo:
# providers ranked by priority, fit into the token budget
providers = [
    {'name': 'selection', 'priority': 1, 'tokens': 200},
    {'name': 'current-file', 'priority': 2, 'tokens': 1500},
    {'name': 'imports', 'priority': 3, 'tokens': 3000},
    {'name': 'docs', 'priority': 4, 'tokens': 2000},
]
BUDGET = 4000
used, included = 0, []
for p in sorted(providers, key=lambda x: x['priority']):
    if used + p['tokens'] <= BUDGET:
        used += p['tokens']
        included.append(p['name'])
print('budget %d: included %s (%d tokens)' % (BUDGET, included, used))
print('@-mentions force inclusion; each provider declares its source (privacy)')

title: Prompt caching
description: Prompt caching reuses the expensive prefix: the system prompt + file context barely changes between requests, so providers cache the prefix's KV state and only process the new suffix. Hit rates are high for chat (same file, follow-up questions) — cutting latency and cost 2-10x. Cache keys include the exact prefix; invalidation is by content change.
mechanism: Cache KV for the stable prefix; new requests reuse it. Key = hash(prefix); invalidate on edit. Providers (Anthropic, etc.) expose it as a feature.
algo: O(suffix) per request instead of O(prefix + suffix). 2-10x savings.

title: Streaming UI
description: Streaming UI renders tokens as they arrive: the response types itself out, with a blinking cursor and a stop button. It feels fast even when total time is the same — perceived latency beats actual. The implementation appends tokens to the render (markdown re-parsed incrementally), handles stop cleanly, and shows the final state identically to non-streamed.
mechanism: SSE/token stream -> incremental append -> markdown re-parse per chunk (or per line) -> stop button aborts. Final render identical to batch.
demo:
import time

# perceived latency: first token fast matters more than total time
tokens = ['The', ' answer', ' streams', ' in.']
start = time.perf_counter()
for i, tok in enumerate(tokens):
    if i == 0:
        print('first token at %.0fms (feels fast)' % ((time.perf_counter()-start)*1000))
    time.sleep(0.05)
print(''.join(tokens), '<- final identical to batch render')
print('stop button aborts cleanly; markdown re-parsed incrementally')

title: Accept/reject UX
description: AI edits need accept/reject UX: proposed changes render as diffs, the user accepts hunks (or all), edits the proposal, or rejects. Partial acceptance is essential — the AI is right about 3 of 4 hunks. The interaction is review, not execution: the user stays the author. Keyboard: accept, reject, next-hunk.
mechanism: Proposal -> diff view -> per-hunk accept/reject -> apply accepted. Edit-the-proposal supported. Never auto-apply without review (configurable for trusted).
algo: O(hunks) review; the UX is the work.
demo:
# per-hunk review: the user stays the author
hunks = [
    {'id': 1, 'desc': 'fix null check', 'good': True},
    {'id': 2, 'desc': 'rename variable', 'good': True},
    {'id': 3, 'desc': 'change algorithm', 'good': False},
]
for h in hunks:
    decision = 'ACCEPT' if h['good'] else 'REJECT (edit manually)'
    print('hunk %d %-16s -> %s' % (h['id'], h['desc'], decision))
print('partial acceptance is essential: right about 3 of 4 hunks')
print('never auto-apply without review (until explicitly trusted)')

title: Privacy modes
description: Privacy modes control what the AI sees: local-only (no code leaves the machine), allowlist (only these repos), blocklist (never these paths), and full-cloud. Regulated industries need the local mode with on-device models. The mode is visible and sticky — users know what is shared. Code snippets in prompts are the leak vector; modes are the control.
mechanism: Modes: local / allowlist / blocklist / full. Enforced at the context-provider layer (providers check the mode before gathering). Visible indicator.

title: Model switching
description: Model switching routes requests to the right model: fast small model for completions, large model for hard chat questions, specialized models for languages. The router considers latency budget, cost, and task type. Users can pin a model; the default is automatic. Switching is invisible when done right — the UX is one assistant, many engines.
mechanism: Router: task type + budget -> model. Completions: small/fast; chat: large; fallback on failure. User pin overrides. One UX, many engines.
algo: O(1) routing; the models do the work.

title: Sidecar latency budgets
description: Sidecar latency budgets are tiered: completions <100ms (or don't show), chat first token <1s, edits <5s. Each tier has a fallback — slow completion becomes no completion (better than late), slow chat shows progress. The budgets are measured per release; regressions block ship. Latency is the feature users feel most.
mechanism: Tiered budgets + fallbacks per tier; measured in CI on reference hardware; regressions block. Degrade: late completion = no completion.

title: Cost controls
description: LLM sidecars cost real money per token: cost controls keep it sustainable — per-user budgets, model routing (cheap for easy), caching (prefix + exact), and rate limits. The dashboard shows spend per team; alerts fire on spikes. The business model decides the controls: per-seat includes a token budget; overage is visible, never silent.
mechanism: Budgets per user/team; routing to cheap models; aggressive caching; rate limits; spend dashboards + alerts. Overage visible.
algo: O(1) checks; caching is the lever.
demo:
# per-user token budget with visible overage
budget, used = 100000, 0

def spend(tokens, user='u1'):
    global used
    if used + tokens > budget:
        return 'BLOCKED: budget exceeded (visible, not silent)'
    used += tokens
    return 'ok (%d/%d used)' % (used, budget)

print(spend(40000))
print(spend(70000))
print('levers: routing (cheap models), caching, rate limits; dashboards per team')

title: Evaluating sidecars
description: Sidecar evaluation is task-based: can the AI complete real tasks (SWE-bench style), what is the acceptance rate on production traffic, do users keep the feature on. mechanism: Benchmarks per model upgrade; replay harnesses on recorded sessions; production acceptance/success metrics; human review of samples. Ship on data.

title: Sidecar accessibility
description: AI sidebars must be accessible: the chat is keyboard-navigable, responses are screen-reader friendly (structured, not just streamed text), ghost text doesn't confuse screen readers (announced carefully or suppressed), and every AI action has a non-AI equivalent. The AI is an enhancement, never the only path.
mechanism: Semantic chat markup; SR announcements for completions (configurable); keyboard parity; non-AI paths preserved. Test with SR users.
